title: The Door of the Seas: the Bank of England, the Company of Scotland, and the Colony at Darien
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Skipmyre, Tinwald: the farmhouse birth
stops.date_confidence: year attested by DNB and Encyclopedia.com; month reported as April by Wikipedia alone and no parish register is reproduced in any source reached, so the day is a default
stops.campa: In a farmhouse at Skipmyre, in the parish of Tinwald a few miles north of Dumfries, a son is born to a tenant family of the Nithsdale border country. The sources part company at once over what happens next. Wikipedia keeps the boy on the farm until he is seventeen; the Dictionary of National Biography says flatly that he was bred in England from his infancy, raised at Bristol by a kinswoman. They agree only on the farm, the shire and the year. The man who will write the founding prospectus of the Bank of England begins in a house that keeps no ledgers.
suggested_refs: The farm of Skipmyre in the parish of Tinwald, Dumfriesshire, named by both DNB and Wikipedia as the birthplace

stops.name: Bristol, the disputed boyhood
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; 'about seventeen' is Wikipedia's phrasing, and the DNB version has him here from infancy instead, which would void the date entirely
stops.campa: Bristol is the second city of English trade, its quays taking sugar and tobacco off the Atlantic passage. One account brings Paterson here at about seventeen, a Scots boy off the Dumfriesshire hills pausing before he sails west. The other has him here since infancy, with a maternal relative, and no Scottish childhood at all. Neither side produces the record that would settle it. On either telling the city shows him one thing worth knowing: money crosses an ocean and comes back larger than it went.
suggested_refs: The Bristol harbourside quays in the 1670s, second port of English Atlantic trade

stops.name: Nassau, New Providence: the merchant among buccaneers
stops.date_confidence: decade attested, year and town both inferred; the source names only 'the Bahamas' and hedges the buccaneer connection with 'it is said'
stops.campa: He crosses to the Bahamas and works as a merchant in the West Indies, in waters where the difference between trade and piracy is a question of whose flag is nearest. The company he keeps there is buccaneer company, men who have walked the isthmus and know where the Spanish silver road runs from Panama to Portobelo. From them, or from the privateer William Dampier, he takes the fact he will spend the rest of his life on: at Darien the two oceans lie sixty miles apart, and no European power holds the ground between them.
suggested_refs: William Dampier's accounts of the Darien isthmus, named by Wikipedia as a possible route by which Paterson learned the geography

stops.name: Merchant Taylors' Hall, London: admitted to the Company
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Dictionary of National Biography
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of November he is admitted to the Merchant Taylors' Company, one of the great livery companies of London. Its freedom is a licence to trade at all, and has little to do with cloth. Under its flag he will run cargoes to the West Indies, and that traffic includes the slave trade. The hall has stood on this ground between Threadneedle Street and Cornhill since 1347. A few hundred yards away, thirteen years from now, he will help charter a bank that is still there when the tailors' broadcloth is a memory.
suggested_refs: The admission rolls of the Merchant Taylors' Company, Threadneedle Street, cited by the DNB for 16 November 1681

stops.name: Golden Island, Darien: the isthmus first imagined
stops.date_confidence: tradition; DNB dates the conception of the scheme to 1684, but no primary account confirms Paterson stood on this coast before 1698
stops.campa: Off the Darien coast lies a low island the buccaneers use as the landmark for the bay behind it. Tradition puts Paterson here among them in these years, learning the isthmus by walking it. The Dictionary of National Biography dates the conception of the colony to 1684; nothing reached in this research places him physically on the shore before the fleet arrives fourteen years later. By the middle of the decade he is carrying from court to court a plan built on this geography: a free port on the neck of the Americas, open to all nations.
suggested_refs: Golden Island (Isla de Oro), the landfall marker for Caledonia Bay in the 1698 sailing orders

stops.name: Whitehall Palace, Westminster: the plan refused by James II
stops.date_confidence: window rather than date; Wikipedia says only 'by the middle 1680s' and James II reigns 1685 to 1688, so the year is a placement inside that window
stops.campa: He brings the plan to the government of James II at Whitehall, and Whitehall refuses it. England has a chartered East India Company and a Royal African Company and no appetite for a Scots projector proposing a free port in territory Spain claims by treaty and by the sword. Wikipedia gives no year for the approach, only the middle of the decade and the fact of the refusal. Paterson treats the refusal as a routing problem rather than a verdict, and sails for the Continent to find a sovereign who will listen.
suggested_refs: The court of James II at Whitehall Palace, first government to be offered the Darien scheme

stops.name: Amsterdam, the Dutch Republic declines
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the source names the Dutch Republic and not the city, and gives no year within the middle 1680s
stops.campa: The Dutch Republic is the place where a scheme like his ought to be understood. The Bank of Amsterdam is eighty years old, the exchange trades shares in a company that governs islands, and the whole apparatus of paper credit he wants to build for somebody already stands here in brick. They hear him out and they decline. He is asking them to plant a colony in the Spanish Main on the strength of a Scotsman's map, and their own East India monopoly is answer enough without any argument about Spain.
suggested_refs: The Wisselbank of Amsterdam, founded 1609, the working model of public banking Paterson would import to London

stops.name: Vienna, the Empire declines
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the source names the Holy Roman Empire without a city or a year, and the imperial seat is the inference
stops.campa: The Holy Roman Empire is approached next, and the imperial seat is where such approaches are made. Vienna in these years has other business. The Turks were at these walls in 1683 and the reconquest of Hungary is being fought southward down the Danube month by month. An emperor fighting on his own frontier has neither a fleet to spare nor a reason to want an isthmus he cannot find on a chart. The plan is declined here as it was at Whitehall, and the projector turns north again.
suggested_refs: The Hofburg court of Leopold I during the Great Turkish War, named in the sources only as 'the Holy Roman Empire'

stops.name: Berlin, Brandenburg declines
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the source names Brandenburg without naming Berlin, and supplies no year
stops.campa: Brandenburg is the last Continental door. The Great Elector has built a small fleet and a fort on the Gold Coast and is the one German prince who has actually tried the Atlantic trade, which is presumably why Paterson comes. The answer is the same answer. Four governments have now examined the Darien plan and four have sent him away, and the man who will one day be told he has a prodigious genius goes back to London to make himself rich enough that the next government has to hear him out.
suggested_refs: The Brandenburg African Company and Gross Friedrichsburg, the elector's Atlantic venture of the 1680s

stops.name: Merchant Taylors' Hall, London: the fortune and the livery
stops.date_confidence: livery admission attested to the day by DNB; the settling in London is dated 1687 by Wikipedia, and the Hampstead Water Company is given no date by any source reached
stops.campa: He settles in London and makes a fortune in foreign trade, and on the twenty-first of October is admitted to the livery of the Merchant Taylors' Company, the rank above the freedom. He also helps found a company to bring water down from the Hampstead hills to the northern parishes, an undertaking that outlives him by nearly two centuries. The company is chartered, the capital is subscribed, and the thing that moves down the channel dug for it is water. In five years he will build the same machine for silver.
suggested_refs: The Hampstead Water Company, founded with Paterson's help and surviving into the late nineteenth century

stops.name: The Royal Exchange, Cornhill: the bank proposed with Michael Godfrey
stops.date_confidence: DNB dates the proposal to July and August 1691; no source names the room in which it was drafted, and the merchants' meeting ground is inferred
stops.campa: In July and August he and Michael Godfrey put a proposal to the government: a national bank, a joint stock lent to the Crown, the debt made permanent and the paper made spendable. He is its chief projector. Nothing is permitted to be done in it for three years. England is at war with France, the war costs more than the land tax will carry, and the proposal keeps in a drawer until the Treasury is desperate enough to open it. Paterson will still be complaining about those three years a quarter of a century later, in print, through a fictional mouthpiece.
suggested_refs: Michael Godfrey, co-projector of 1691 and first deputy governor of the Bank, killed at the siege of Namur in 1695

stops.name: The Palace of Westminster: the principal witness
stops.date_confidence: month attested by DNB, day defaulted
stops.campa: A parliamentary committee sits on the question of how to raise supplies for the war against France, and Paterson appears before it as principal witness. He is a Scot with no seat, no office and no title, explaining to the Commons of England how a state might borrow against its own future taxes forever instead of pawning next year's customs. It is the first time the scheme is heard by the body that can enact it. The Commons take it up as a way to pay for ships needed this season, and not as a theory of money.
suggested_refs: The Commons committee on ways of raising supplies for the French war, January 1692

stops.name: London, A Brief Account of the Intended Bank of England
stops.date_confidence: year given by the Bank of England; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: The tract goes out anonymously and it is the founding prospectus of a bank that does not yet exist. It argues that London, the richest trading city in the world, has no public fund for great payments, and that the want of one has cost the merchants millions in unnecessary credit. It sets out the subscription, the security, the return. Saxe Bannister will print it a century and a half later from the copy in the King's Collection at the British Museum. The Bank of England dates the pamphlet to 1694, three years after the proposal it argues for.
stops.quote: The want of a bank, or public fund for the convenience and security of great payments, and the better to facilitate the circulation of money in and about this great and opulent city, hath in our time, among other inconveniences, occasioned much unnecessary credit, to the loss of several millions, by which trade hath been exceedingly discouraged and obstructed.
stops.quote_source: William Paterson, 'A Brief Account of the Intended Bank of England' (anonymous tract, London, 1694), in The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (London: Judd and Glass, 1859), vol. III, p. 80
suggested_refs: The copy of the 1694 tract in the King's Collection, British Museum, from which Bannister printed his text
sources: The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. III

stops.name: The Palace of Westminster: the Tonnage Act
stops.date_confidence: royal assent to the enabling act is given in April 1694; the day is defaulted, and the sources reached conflate this assent with the separate grant of the charter in July
stops.campa: The enabling statute passes: a duty laid on ships and on beer, and the subscribers of a loan of 1,200,000 pounds to the Crown granted the right to be incorporated. The instrument is not elegant. It is a war tax with a bank folded into it, the price England pays for a fleet it cannot otherwise fund, and the corporation it authorises is chartered as a means to that end. The means will outlast every purpose for which it was raised, and the war it was raised for will be over in three years.
suggested_refs: The Tonnage Act 1694, the statute under which the Bank of England was incorporated

stops.name: Mercers' Hall, Cheapside: the books filled and the charter granted
stops.date_confidence: charter date attested to the day; the subscription is attested as twelve days but not dated precisely, and the Bank opened for business on 1 August
stops.campa: The subscription book opens at Mercers' Hall on Cheapside and the whole 1,200,000 pounds is taken in twelve days by 1,268 subscribers, women among them. On the twenty-seventh of July the Crown grants the charter under the Great Seal and the Governor and Company of the Bank of England exists; the doors open for business five days later. Paterson is one of the founding directors, holding the 2,000 pounds of stock the office requires. In Vienna, Samuel Oppenheimer has just come out of two years in prison, and the age of the court financier who lends an emperor his own fortune begins to give way to this.
stops.quote: This bank will consist in a revenue or income of eight per cent. per annum, for and upon the money subscribed.
stops.quote_source: William Paterson, 'A Brief Account of the Intended Bank of England' (1694), in The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. III, p. 84
suggested_refs: The Bank of England subscription book of June 1694, opened at Mercers' Hall and filled in twelve days

stops.name: Grocers' Hall, Poultry: the Bank moves house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Bank of England's own institutional history
stops.campa: On the last day of the year the Bank moves from the mercers' rooms to Grocers' Hall on Poultry, where it will sit for nearly forty years. Its notes are circulating already, paper that promises silver and is accepted as silver, and the promise is worth exactly what the coin behind it is worth. Paterson has written in the prospectus that money without an intrinsic value to answer its denomination is false and counterfeit, and that the loss must fall somewhere. Within eighteen months the clipped and debased silver of England will test that sentence to destruction.
stops.quote: All money or credit not having an intrinsic value, to answer the contents or denomination thereof, is false and counterfeit; and the loss must fall one where or other.
stops.quote_source: William Paterson, 'A Brief Account of the Intended Bank of England' (1694), in The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. III, p. 83
suggested_refs: Grocers' Hall on Poultry, home of the Bank of England from 1694 to 1734

stops.name: Grocers' Hall, Poultry: the founder withdraws
stops.date_confidence: year only; both Wikipedia and DNB give 1695 without a month, and neither states the substance of the disagreement
stops.campa: He quarrels with his fellow directors and withdraws from the court, a year or so after the charter. The bank is not his any more; it belongs to the City. What follows he watches from outside. Isaac Newton takes the wardenship of the Royal Mint in the Tower in 1696 and runs the Great Recoinage that rebuilds the silver under the paper, with Edmond Halley keeping the books of the branch mint at Chester, while John Locke argues the standard from the Board of Trade at Whitehall. The institution Paterson designed is rescued by three men he never sat in a room with.
suggested_refs: The Great Recoinage of 1696 and the currency crisis that tested the two-year-old Bank of England

stops.name: Parliament Close, Edinburgh: the Act of the twenty-sixth of June
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by DNB
stops.campa: He goes north. On the twenty-sixth of June the Parliament of Scotland passes the Act he has drafted, erecting the Company of Scotland Trading to Africa and the Indies, with power to plant colonies in places not possessed by any European sovereign, a monopoly of twenty-one years and freedom from customs. Scotland has no navy, no colonies and no bullion. It has instead a statute written by a man who has spent ten years being refused by four governments that had all three, and who has now gone and had one written to order.
suggested_refs: The Act for a Company Trading to Africa and the Indies, Parliament of Scotland, 26 June 1695

stops.name: London, the letters to the Lord Provost
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; Bannister prints letters of 4 and 9 July 1695 in his biographical introduction
stops.campa: He is in London raising English capital for the Scottish company and writing north to the Lord Provost of Edinburgh in the register of a man who knows he is being watched. Keep private and close for some months, he writes, so that the Parliament of England is given no occasion to take notice of it in the coming session; a great many considerable persons are already alarmed. They are alarmed. The English East India interest reads a Scots company holding a twenty-one year monopoly as a hole cut in its own wall, and it has friends in both houses.
stops.quote: The gentlemen here think that we ought to keep private and close for some months, that no occasion may be given to the Parliament of England to take notice of it in the ensuing Session, which might be of ill consequence, especially as a great many considerable persons are already alarmed at it.
stops.quote_source: William Paterson, letter to the Lord Provost of Edinburgh, 9 July 1695, printed in the Darien Papers and quoted in The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I, p. xxxviii
suggested_refs: The Darien Papers, containing Paterson's London correspondence with the Lord Provost of Edinburgh, summer 1695
sources: The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I, Biographical Introduction

stops.name: London, the third of September and the last optimism
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Bannister
stops.campa: In September he is still confident. He writes that the business has taken more than they expected, and that the politicians in London seem inclined to have England follow the Scottish example in encouraging foreign trade rather than to think of discouraging it. He is wrong. Before the year ends the House of Lords is examining the company, the English subscribers are frightened off, and the Dutch and Hamburg money leaves with them. The foreign capital the venture was designed on evaporates under pressure from the government whose bank he built.
stops.quote: Our business hath taken more than we expected... Our politicians here seem inclined rather to endeavour that England should follow our example as much as may be, in encouraging foreign trade, than to think of discouraging us, who, if blessed with prudent management, have designed one of the least involved and freest foundations of commerce anywhere proposed.
stops.quote_source: William Paterson, letter to the Lord Provost of Edinburgh, 3 September 1695, printed in the Darien Papers and quoted in The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I, p. xxxix
suggested_refs: The English parliamentary inquiry of late 1695 into the Company of Scotland's English subscribers
sources: The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I

stops.name: Parliament Close, Edinburgh: the subscription book opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Company of Scotland record
stops.campa: With the foreign money gone the books open in Edinburgh on the twenty-sixth of February, and Scotland subscribes to the scheme itself. By the beginning of August the full 400,000 pounds sterling is reached, taken from a country whose own historians reckon it put in something like a quarter of its liquid assets. Nobles, burghs, merchants, lairds and widows sign for what they have. Paterson had written the summer before exactly how such a book must be run: opened short, closed hot, the multitude led more by example than by reason.
stops.quote: The Bank of England had but six weeks' time for opening the books, and was finished in nine days. In all subscriptions here it is always limited to a short day. If a thing go not off with the first heat, the raising a fund seldom or never succeeds, the multitude being mainly led more by example than by reason.
stops.quote_source: William Paterson, letter to the Lord Provost of Edinburgh, 9 July 1695, printed in the Darien Papers and quoted in The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I, pp. xxxviii-xxxix
suggested_refs: The Company of Scotland subscription book, opened in Edinburgh 26 February 1696
sources: The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I

stops.name: Trongate, Glasgow: the second book
stops.date_confidence: attested; the book was open from 5 March to 22 April 1696
stops.campa: A second book opens in Glasgow and stays open from the fifth of March to the twenty-second of April. Glasgow is a small tobacco port on a river too shallow for the ships it wants, a town whose merchants have every reason to believe that a Scottish company trading on its own account would make them. They subscribe. Nothing in the surviving record suggests that any subscriber in either city is told four European governments have already read this plan and handed it back.
suggested_refs: The Glasgow subscription book of the Company of Scotland, 5 March to 22 April 1696

stops.name: Mylne Square, Edinburgh: the company's offices
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the court of directors meets here from July 1696
stops.campa: From July the court of directors meets in the company's own offices in Mylne Square on Edinburgh's High Street. Here the ships are commissioned, the stores contracted and the officers named. Paterson is not one of the directors who sit in this room; his standing in the company is that of the man whose idea it is, which in a joint stock is not an office. He had written to the Provost that they must not act apart in anything, but in a firm and united body, distinct from all interest whatever. The court will read that sentence in its own way.
stops.quote: We must not act apart in anything, but in a firm and united body, and distinct from all interest whatever.
stops.quote_source: William Paterson, letter to the Lord Provost of Edinburgh, c. 9 July 1695, printed in the Darien Papers and quoted in The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I, p. xxxix
suggested_refs: Mylne Square on Edinburgh's High Street, headquarters of the Company of Scotland from July 1696
sources: The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I

stops.name: Hamburg, the foreign money gone and the stores bought
stops.date_confidence: year attested by DNB, which places him abroad as a director commissioned to buy stores; the city is inferred from the Hamburg and Amsterdam subscription attempts
stops.campa: He works the Continent for the company through the year, a director abroad, commissioned to purchase stores for an expedition whose destination is still officially secret. Hamburg and Amsterdam had been meant to supply capital and are now only markets: English residents have warned both senates off any dealing with the Scots. What he sends home is provisions and trade goods bought against a deadline by men who have never victualled a colony in the tropics. The Dictionary of National Biography records the commission and not one item of the manifest.
suggested_refs: English diplomatic pressure on Hamburg and Amsterdam against the Company of Scotland, 1696-1697

stops.name: Port of Leith, Edinburgh: five ships sail
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Encyclopedia.com and the Darien scheme record
stops.campa: Five ships lie at Leith: Saint Andrew, Caledonia, Unicorn, Dolphin and Endeavour. On the fourteenth of July they sail with about 1,200 colonists aboard, and the crowd on the shore is the size of a national occasion. Paterson sails with them, and his wife Hannah Kemp and their child sail with him. The orders naming the destination are sealed and are not opened until the fleet is at sea. He is forty years old and has spent half his life persuading somebody to fund this hour. Nobody aboard has ever governed a colony.
suggested_refs: The five ships of the first Darien expedition, fitted out at Leith in the summer of 1698

stops.name: Funchal, Madeira: the last European harbour
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day inferred from the sailing date and the passage time
stops.campa: The fleet calls at Madeira on the crossing, taking on water and wine at a Portuguese island that has been an Atlantic waystation since before Columbus. It is the last European harbour any of them will see. From Funchal the run is southwest across the trades toward the Caribbean, weeks of open water with the ships already crowded and the sickness already started. The colony has not begun and the arithmetic of the voyage has begun subtracting from it. Nothing in the sources records how many were buried between Funchal and the Antilles.
suggested_refs: Funchal, Madeira, victualling stop of the Darien fleet on the Atlantic crossing

stops.name: Vieques, Puerto Rico: Crab Island claimed
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is not, and must precede the 2 November landfall at Darien, so October is a placement and not a record
stops.campa: Off Puerto Rico the expedition takes possession of Crab Island, which the Danes call Vieques and also claim. A Scottish company carrying a Scottish statute in its hold asserts a title over ground the crowns of Europe have already divided among themselves, and every one of those crowns keeps a fleet. The claim is made, entered, and never enforced. The ships do not stay. The isthmus is what they came for, and the isthmus is a week to the southwest across the Caribbean.
suggested_refs: The Danish West India Company's competing claim to Crab Island (Vieques)

stops.name: Caledonia Bay, Darien: Fort St Andrew raised
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the second of November the fleet raises the Darien coast and works into the bay behind Golden Island. They name the country Caledonia, throw up Fort St Andrew with fifty guns commanding the entrance, and lay out the streets of New Edinburgh. The harbour is superb. The site is a swamp with no dependable fresh water. Two and a quarter centuries later Aime Tschiffely, riding two Criollo horses from Buenos Aires toward Washington, will refuse this ground outright and ship the animals around it by sea, because the Darien defeats horses absolutely.
stops.quote: Thus these doors of the seas and the keys of the universe would of course be capable of enabling their possessors to give laws to both oceans, and to become the arbitrators of the commercial world, without being liable to the fatigues, expenses, and dangers, or of contracting such guilt and blood, as Alexander and Caesar.
stops.quote_source: William Paterson, 'A Proposal to Plant a Colony in Darien' (1701), in The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I, p. 159, written three years after this landfall
suggested_refs: Fort St Andrew and New Edinburgh at Caledonia Bay, raised November 1698
sources: The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I

stops.name: Caledonia Bay, Darien: the winter and the graves
stops.date_confidence: winter of 1698-1699; the sources place the deaths of Hannah Kemp and the child in the colony after the November landfall but give no day, and the chronology lens had dated them a year early
stops.campa: The rain comes and does not stop. Fever takes the settlers by the day, the salt provisions rot, the Spanish close the coast, and the English colonies are under standing orders from London to sell them nothing. Hannah Kemp and the child die here; the Dictionary of National Biography records an earlier wife, Elizabeth Turner, dead before her. Paterson lies seriously ill through it. In July the survivors abandon the fort after some eight months, having buried about 900 of the 1,200 who sailed from Leith.
suggested_refs: The burial ground of the first Caledonia colony, abandoned July 1699

stops.name: New York Harbor: the Caledonia comes in
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The Caledonia comes into New York on the tenth of August with about 250 survivors aboard, the Unicorn four days behind her. Paterson lands in an English colony that had been forbidden to relieve him, carrying nothing: no wife, no child, no colony, and no standing with the court of directors, which has already turned against him over money embezzled by a subordinate he vouched for. He is forty-one. The plan four governments refused has now been tried with a small nation's savings and it has killed nine hundred people.
suggested_refs: The Caledonia and the Unicorn at New York, August 1699, carrying the survivors of the first colony

stops.name: Parliament Close, Edinburgh: the return in December
stops.date_confidence: DNB gives 5 December 1699; Wikipedia and Encyclopedia.com give December without a day
stops.campa: He is back in Edinburgh in December, in a city that has lost its money and wants to know whose fault it is. Scotland's answer is England, and the answer is not wrong: the withdrawal of the foreign capital, the orders to the colonial governors, the refusal of relief were all English acts. A second wave of over a thousand settlers is at that moment sailing to the graveyard he left, where they will take the Spanish stockade at Toubacanti and then lose the colony for good. Paterson neither defends himself in print nor attacks the company.
suggested_refs: The second Darien expedition of 1699-1700 and the storming of Toubacanti

stops.name: Edinburgh, a prodigious genius
stops.date_confidence: the underlying letter is dated 14 September 1700 in Bannister's preface; the epigraph itself is printed with the year alone
stops.campa: A correspondent writing from Edinburgh into the papers of William Carstares, the king's chaplain and the manager of Scottish business, sets down one sentence about the ruined projector that will outlive everything else said of him in his lifetime. Bannister prints it on the title page of all three volumes of the collected writings and attributes it to T. Stewart. Carstares is the man the letters were sent to, not the man who wrote them, and the confusion of the two has followed the quotation ever since it was first reprinted.
stops.quote_source: T. Stewart, Edinburgh, 1700, in The Carstares Correspondence, p. 436, printed as the epigraph on the title page of The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (London: Judd and Glass, 1859), vol. I
suggested_refs: The Carstares Correspondence, whose pagination Bannister cites variously as 436, 633 and 646 for the same sequence of letters
sources: The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I, title page and Editor's Preface

stops.name: London, A Proposal to Plant a Colony in Darien
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: He publishes the Darien plan again, now that it has failed, as a proposal to plant a colony to protect the Indians against Spain and open the trade of South America to all nations. The prose is not chastened. Trade increases trade and money begets money to the end of the world; the isthmus is the door of the seas and the key of the universe, and whoever holds it gives law to both oceans without the guilt and blood of Alexander or Caesar. A hundred and fourteen years later Simon Bolivar, writing from Kingston, imagines the same neck of land gathering the American nations into one commerce.
stops.quote: Trade is capable of increasing trade, and money of begetting money to the end of the world.
stops.quote_source: William Paterson, 'A Proposal to Plant a Colony in Darien, to Protect the Indians against Spain, and to Open the Trade of South America to All Nations' (1701), in The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. I, p. 158
suggested_refs: The 1701 Darien proposal, the tract that carried Paterson's most quoted sentences

stops.name: The Palace of Westminster: received by King William
stops.date_confidence: month attested by DNB, day defaulted
stops.campa: In April he is received by King William and consulted on questions of public credit. The king chartered his bank in 1694 and, through his English ministers, strangled his company in 1696; he is now asking the same man how a state should be funded. Paterson takes the audience. A projector who is being listened to by a king does not spend the hour on grievance. William is dead within a year, and whatever was owed to Paterson for Darien passes into the paperwork of the next reign, where it will sit for fourteen years.
suggested_refs: Paterson's audience with William III on public credit, April 1701

stops.name: The Cockpit, Whitehall: the Equivalent computed
stops.date_confidence: year attested for Paterson's employment on the Equivalent; the commission sits at the Cockpit from April 1706, and no source reached confirms Paterson was physically present in that room
stops.campa: The commissioners for the Union meet at the Cockpit in Whitehall, and the hardest article is money: what Scotland is owed for taking on a share of England's national debt. The sum is called the Equivalent, and a large part of it is set aside to repay the Darien subscribers. Paterson does the calculation and helps frame the articles on trade and finance. In these same Whitehall rooms John Locke had sat on the Board of Trade a decade earlier, ruling on the coinage, the colonies and the terms of trade, in the years the Company of Scotland was being killed.
suggested_refs: The 1706 Union commission at the Cockpit, Whitehall, and the computation of the Equivalent

stops.name: Parliament Close, Edinburgh: the last recommendation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by DNB
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of March, days before it dissolves itself forever, the Parliament of Scotland formally recommends Paterson's services and his losses to Queen Anne. It is the last business of a legislature voting itself out of existence, and one of its closing gestures is to point at the man whose company ruined the country and record that he is owed. The recommendation carries no money with it. It is a character reference issued by a body that will not exist to enforce it, addressed to a crown that has no obligation to read it.
suggested_refs: The final session of the Parliament of Scotland, March 1707

stops.name: The Palace of Westminster: the Union takes effect
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the first of May the Acts of Union take effect and the two parliaments become one at Westminster. The Equivalent money goes north in wagons under guard and is stoned in the Edinburgh streets on its way in. Paterson is now the author of England's public bank and of Scotland's public catastrophe, and the settlement that joins the two kingdoms is built partly out of the wreckage of the second, on terms he calculated himself. He is forty-nine and holds no office in the kingdom he has helped to assemble.
suggested_refs: The Acts of Union 1707 and the carriage of the Equivalent to Edinburgh

segments.name: Queen Square and the Long Afterward

stops.name: The Palace of Westminster: the bill the Lords throw out
stops.date_confidence: year attested by DNB, which records the Commons passing the bill and the Lords rejecting it without giving a month
stops.campa: The Commons pass a bill awarding him 18,000 pounds for his Darien losses, and the Lords throw it out. He has been petitioning since the Union on the strength of a dissolved parliament's recommendation, in a chamber where Scottish claims arrive at the bottom of the order paper. The Dictionary of National Biography records the passage and the rejection and not one word of the reason. He is fifty-five, and the argument he is making is that a man may be a creditor of a state whose credit he invented.
suggested_refs: The indemnity bill of 1713, passed by the Commons and rejected by the Lords

stops.name: The Palace of Westminster: eighteen thousand pounds
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is not given, and the sources report the sum as 'roughly' 18,000 pounds
stops.campa: Parliament grants the indemnity at last, reported as roughly 18,000 pounds, sixteen years after the Caledonia came into New York. It is the same figure the Lords rejected in 1713. Only the Parliament has changed: a new king sits, the Union is old enough to settle its arrears, and the Darien subscribers have mostly been paid through the Equivalent already. Whether the money reached him whole, or in instalments, or against what deductions, no source consulted in this research says. He is fifty-seven.
suggested_refs: The 1715 parliamentary indemnity to Paterson for his Darien losses

stops.name: London, the Wednesday's Club dialogues
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: He publishes dialogues on the Union set in a club that meets on Wednesdays and puts the case for the Bank into the mouth of a member called Mr. May, who recalls that the proposition was first made in July and August 1691, was so ill received that nothing was permitted to be done in it for three years, and then but lamely. Bannister reads Mr. May as Paterson himself. No independent evidence that the club existed survives. The model those three years produced crosses the Atlantic; Alexis de Tocqueville will watch Andrew Jackson veto its American copy in 1832, and Abraham Lincoln's currency act of 1863 will fill the hole Jackson made.
stops.quote: The proposition of the Bank was first made in the months of July and August, 1691; and was so far from being well received, nothing was permitted to be done in it till three years after, and then but lamely neither, and far from the extensive nature and other public advantages concerted in the proposition.
stops.quote_source: William Paterson (speaking as 'Mr. May'), Wednesday's Club Dialogues upon the Union of Great Britain (London, 1717), in The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. II, pp. 63-64
suggested_refs: Wednesday's Club Dialogues upon the Union of Great Britain (1717), Paterson's late apologia for the Bank
sources: The Writings of William Paterson, ed. Saxe Bannister, 2nd ed. (1859), vol. II

stops.name: Queen Square, Westminster: the death and the will
stops.date_confidence: DNB and Wikipedia give only January 1719 for the death; the 22 January often printed as the death date is the date the will was proved at Doctors' Commons, Old Style, and one Scottish source states it as the death date outright
stops.campa: He dies in January at his house in Queen Square, Westminster, where the Dictionary of National Biography places him from 1703. The will is proved at Doctors' Commons on the twenty-second of the month by Old Style reckoning, and that date has since been printed in several places as the date of his death. He is sixty. The bank he projected is twenty-five years old and holds the debt of a state that has become a great power. The colony he projected has been jungle for twenty years.
suggested_refs: The probate of Paterson's will at Doctors' Commons, London, 22 January 1719 Old Style

stops.name: Sweetheart Abbey, New Abbey: the grave nobody can prove
stops.date_confidence: the burial is undated and unlocated; the abbey is a tradition, and the 1719 date is the year of death carried across to it
stops.campa: Nobody can say where he is buried. The tradition, held among others by officers of the Bank of England, puts him in the graveyard of Sweetheart Abbey at New Abbey, twenty miles from the farm where he was born. Wikipedia calls the location an open mystery. One Scottish tertiary site states the burial as settled fact, and the same site calls him Sir William Paterson throughout, a knighthood no record supports. A commemorative plaque was unveiled at the abbey in 1974. It marks a grave that has never been identified.
suggested_refs: The 1974 commemorative plaque at Sweetheart Abbey, New Abbey, Dumfries and Galloway

stops.name: Tinwald Top, Dumfriesshire: the cairn never built
stops.date_confidence: the antiquarian volume is undated in the digitized copy consulted; the nineteenth-century placement is a reconstruction and the fate of the proposal is unknown
stops.campa: A nineteenth-century antiquarian volume proposes a memorial to Paterson at Skipmyre farmhouse or on the ridge of Tinwald Top, some seven hundred feet up between Nithsdale and Annandale, calling it potentially a thing of beauty and an object of attraction. Nothing found in this research shows it was ever built. The ridge carries no cairn for the man who wrote the founding prospectus of the Bank of England, and whether the proposal was refused, abandoned, or never more than a paragraph is a gap the sources do not close.
suggested_refs: 'Histories of Scottish Families', p. 73, digitized by the National Library of Scotland
sources: National Library of Scotland, digitized 'Histories of Scottish Families', p. 73

stops.name: Puerto Inabaginya, Guna Yala: the ditch
stops.date_confidence: attested year of the renaming; the survival of the ditch is a present-day observation with no date attached
stops.campa: The place is called Puerto Escoces for three centuries and is renamed Puerto Inabaginya in 2011. A ditch is the only identifiable physical remnant of the settlement in the ground. What Darien left elsewhere lasts better: Eliot Warburton's novel of 1852, Douglas Galbraith's fictional journal of 2000, Alistair Beaton's play of 2010, a song by the Paul McKenna Band, a boardgame by the Ragnar Brothers, and an audiovisual installation by Kode9 and Lawrence Lek shown in London in 2021. The Bank of England is in its fourth century.
suggested_refs: The site of Fort St Andrew at Puerto Inabaginya, Guna Yala, Panama
